# Modulating Plasma Metal Ions for Cardiovascular Prevention and Treatment: What Human Clinical Evidence Supports

Therapeutic modulation of metal status can be clinically useful, but it is not a general cardiovascular strategy. The strongest evidence supports correcting iron deficiency with intravenous iron in selected patients with symptomatic heart failure, where treatment mainly reduces recurrent heart-failure hospitalizations; mortality benefit remains uncertain. Magnesium replacement is feasible and can modestly lower blood pressure or reduce postoperative atrial fibrillation, but it has not been shown to prevent myocardial infarction or stroke. Routine calcium, zinc, selenium, copper, or high-dose multivitamin supplementation is unsupported for cardiovascular prevention, and calcium may carry a myocardial-infarction hazard signal. EDTA chelation lowers blood lead but did not reduce events in TACT2, failing to replicate the modest benefit reported by TACT ([TACT](https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama/fullarticle/1672238); [TACT2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11325247/); [2025 intravenous-iron meta-analysis](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41591-025-03671-1)).

Reducing exposure to lead, cadmium, arsenic, and other toxic metals is a plausible and important preventive measure, particularly at population level, but direct randomized evidence that exposure reduction prevents cardiovascular events is limited. The clinical conclusion is therefore narrow: treat a documented deficiency or poisoning, and use metal-directed therapy only where the underlying cardiovascular indication and outcome evidence justify it.

## Roadmap

The assessment first distinguishes biological plausibility, observational association, genetic evidence, biomarker response, and demonstrated clinical benefit. It then catalogs interventions that raise, lower, bind, remove, or functionally redistribute metal ions. Supplementation is examined by metal, formulation, dose, duration, population, measured concentration, cardiovascular endpoint, and safety. The established-disease section compares TACT, TACT2, IRONMAN, intravenous-iron trials, and iron-depletion studies. The final sections address monitoring, adherence, interactions, contraindications, practical availability, candidate subgroups, and the evidence gaps that prevent routine plasma-metal optimization.

## 1. Plasma metal ions: mechanism, measurement, and the evidence distinction

### What is being targeted?

“Plasma metal concentration” can mean several different biological quantities. A laboratory may report total serum or plasma magnesium, zinc, copper, selenium, calcium, or iron, while the biologically active fraction may be ionized, protein-bound, intracellular, stored in tissue, or incorporated into enzymes. For toxic metals, the clinically relevant specimen may not be plasma at all: venous whole-blood lead, urine cadmium, urine arsenic speciation, and species-specific blood or urine mercury are usually more informative than a generic plasma value.

This distinction matters because changing a circulating measurement is not equivalent to correcting the pathological compartment. Magnesium illustrates the problem. Less than 1% of total body magnesium is in blood, so serum magnesium can underestimate intracellular depletion. Ionized magnesium may be closer to the active fraction, but it is not routinely measured and is sensitive to pH, calcium concentration, specimen type, refrigeration, and freeze–thaw handling ([magnesium supplementation biomarker trial](https://doi.org/10.3390/nu12010263); [2025 magnesium meta-analysis](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12529988/)).

A useful causal chain therefore has at least four stages:

1. The intervention changes exposure, intake, binding, excretion, or tissue availability.
2. The relevant metal biomarker changes.
3. A biological intermediate changes, such as blood pressure, endothelial function, iron stores, or arrhythmia susceptibility.
4. Cardiovascular events, symptoms, function, hospitalization, or mortality improve.

Most metal-ion research reaches only the first two stages. Some reaches the third. Far fewer studies demonstrate the fourth.

### Why the mechanisms are plausible

Metal ions participate in mitochondrial respiration, redox regulation, calcium signaling, vascular tone, electrical conduction, oxygen transport, and inflammatory pathways. Magnesium is a cofactor in hundreds of enzymatic reactions and affects vascular smooth-muscle tone, cardiac rhythm, ATP production, and calcium handling. Iron is essential for hemoglobin and mitochondrial respiration, but excess catalytically active iron can promote oxidative injury. Calcium controls contraction, coagulation, and cellular signaling, yet excessive transient or tissue calcium may contribute to vascular calcification.

Zinc, copper, and selenium have similarly narrow physiological windows. Zinc and copper support antioxidant enzymes and vascular signaling, but excess zinc can cause copper deficiency and excess copper can promote oxidative injury. Selenium is incorporated into selenoproteins involved in redox control and thyroid function, but higher circulating selenium does not necessarily mean greater selenoprotein activity. In selenium-replete populations, supplements may increase selenomethionine without increasing functional selenoproteins ([selenium and coronary disease review](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC1829306/)).

The biological rationale for toxic-metal reduction is stronger in one respect: lead, cadmium, and arsenic have no required physiological role at environmental exposure levels. They can promote oxidative stress, chronic inflammation, endothelial dysfunction, hypertension, dyslipidemia, altered myocardial excitation, and vascular remodeling. The American Heart Association links these exposures with ischemic heart disease, stroke, left-ventricular hypertrophy, heart failure, and peripheral artery disease ([American Heart Association scientific statement](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37306302/)).

These mechanisms justify prevention and clinical investigation. They do not establish that raising or lowering a plasma concentration will improve outcomes in an otherwise replete patient.

### What observational studies show

The observational signal for toxic metals is substantial. A systematic review of 37 studies involving 348,259 participants found that, comparing the highest with the lowest thirds of exposure, cardiovascular-disease risk was higher with arsenic, lead, cadmium, and copper: pooled relative risks were 1.30, 1.43, 1.33, and 1.81, respectively. Mercury was not associated with cardiovascular disease in that analysis, with a pooled relative risk of 0.94 (95% confidence interval 0.66–1.36). For coronary heart disease, the corresponding relative risks were 1.23 for arsenic, 1.85 for lead, 1.29 for cadmium, 2.22 for copper, and 0.99 for mercury ([BMJ systematic review](https://doi.org/10.1136/bmj.k3310)).

Dose-response analyses were compatible with a roughly linear association for arsenic, lead, and cadmium. For example, coronary-heart-disease risk increased by 7% per 5 μg/dL increment in blood lead, while cardiovascular-disease risk increased by 21% per 0.75 μg/g increment in urinary cadmium. These values describe exposure-associated risk, not the benefit that would result from lowering the exposure.

The exposure burden is clinically important. The World Health Organization reports an Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation estimate of 1.5 million global deaths attributable to lead exposure in 2021, primarily cardiovascular deaths ([WHO lead guidance](https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789240078130)). That estimate supports environmental prevention and regulatory action. It does not show that chelation or any supplement will prevent those deaths.

### Why association is not intervention evidence

Metal status is strongly entangled with the determinants of cardiovascular disease. Smoking raises cadmium exposure and independently raises cardiovascular risk. Diet affects magnesium, selenium, zinc, copper, calcium, and mercury simultaneously. Socioeconomic conditions influence housing, water, occupational exposure, nutrition, smoking, healthcare access, and cardiovascular treatment. Kidney disease alters the handling of magnesium, selenium, copper, and toxic metals while also increasing cardiovascular risk.

Reverse causation is equally important. Established cardiovascular disease can cause inflammation, weight loss, reduced food intake, renal dysfunction, altered albumin binding, medication changes, and hospitalization. These processes can change measured metal concentrations without the metal having caused the disease. A low serum magnesium level in a patient with heart failure may therefore be a marker of diuretic use, poor intake, renal or gastrointestinal loss, or illness severity rather than an isolated causal risk factor.

Measurement can distort the association. Spot urine arsenic and cadmium vary with hydration and urinary flow; blood lead reflects recent circulating lead more than the large skeletal reservoir; serum copper and zinc are influenced by albumin and inflammatory proteins; ferritin rises with inflammation and may obscure iron deficiency. Different studies also use different matrices, assays, specimen handling, and exposure windows. The BMJ review specifically cautioned that biomarkers differ in biological determinants, precision, reproducibility, and ability to represent long-term exposure.

### Genetic evidence is informative but not equivalent to supplementation

Mendelian-randomization studies can reduce some confounding and reverse-causation problems by using inherited genetic variants as instruments. A study using six serum-magnesium genetic instruments estimated an odds ratio for coronary artery disease of 0.88 per 0.1 mmol/L higher genetically predicted serum magnesium. Weighted-median and heterogeneity-penalized estimates were similar, but the MR-Egger estimate was imprecise and did not demonstrate a causal association ([magnesium Mendelian-randomization study](https://doi.org/10.1186/s12916-018-1065-z)).

This result supports magnesium as a candidate for trials, especially in people at risk of hypomagnesemia. It does not establish that taking an oral magnesium salt will produce the same lifelong exposure pattern, in the same tissues, with the same effect.

A broader 2024 multi-omics study examined 13 trace elements and 20 cardiovascular diseases using genetic instruments, but many “exposures” were dietary-recall measures rather than directly measured plasma concentrations. Initial analyses associated genetically predicted magnesium and potassium with lower ischemic-heart-disease risk, calcium with myocardial infarction, and higher zinc intake with cardiac arrest. In multivariable analyses, the magnesium and potassium associations with ischemic heart disease became nonsignificant, while the zinc association with cardiac arrest remained. These findings are hypothesis-generating rather than supplementation trials ([multi-omics Mendelian-randomization study](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/immunology/articles/10.3389/fimmu.2024.1459465/full)).

Lead provides a particularly clear example of discordant causal signals. A 13-SNP Mendelian-randomization analysis found no association between genetically instrumented blood lead and coronary artery disease: odds ratio 1.01 per log-transformed blood-lead effect-size unit. The authors noted that genetic instruments might not represent exogenous exposure or total lead burden, particularly lead stored in bone ([lead Mendelian-randomization study](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-019-52482-1)).

The evidence hierarchy therefore remains:

- Mechanistic and animal evidence establishes plausibility.
- Observational evidence identifies associations and vulnerable populations.
- Genetic evidence can strengthen or weaken causal hypotheses.
- Randomized trials determine whether changing status improves clinical outcomes.

Only the last category can justify routine cardiovascular treatment.

## 2. Proposed concentration-modulating interventions

The proposed strategies are not interchangeable. Some increase intake, some restore deficiency, some change metal availability without changing total plasma concentration, and some remove multiple metals simultaneously.

| Intervention | Direction and target | Intended cardiovascular use | Human clinical maturity | Principal limitation |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Oral or intravenous repletion | Raises or restores magnesium, iron, calcium, zinc, selenium, copper, or potassium status | Deficiency, heart failure, hypertension, arrhythmia, or nutritional support | Established for selected deficiencies; cardiovascular benefit varies by metal | No validated cardiovascular target for most ions |
| High-dose multivitamin/mineral therapy | Raises intake of multiple essential metals and vitamins | Primary or secondary prevention of atherosclerotic disease | Tested in TACT; no significant event reduction | Cannot identify the active component; adherence was poor |
| EDTA chelation | Binds and increases urinary removal of lead, calcium, magnesium, zinc, iron, and other cations | Atherosclerotic disease and toxic-metal poisoning | Established for selected poisonings; unapproved for coronary disease | Nonselective metal removal, renal injury, hypocalcemia, long infusions |
| DMSA, DMPS, dimercaprol, and related chelators | Bind selected toxic metals and enhance excretion | Lead, inorganic mercury, arsenic, and severe poisoning | Clinically used for specific toxicology indications | Species-specific efficacy, adverse effects, and limited cardiovascular-outcome evidence |
| Phlebotomy | Lowers circulating red-cell mass and iron stores | Hemochromatosis or experimental iron-reduction strategies | Established for iron overload; cardiovascular prevention unproven | Can cause anemia and may alter other trace metals |
| Source reduction | Lowers ongoing toxic-metal exposure rather than deliberately targeting plasma | Lead, cadmium, arsenic, mercury, and occupational exposure | Strong public-health rationale; cardiovascular event trials sparse | Benefits depend on infrastructure, adherence, and exposure kinetics |
| Vitamin K supplementation | Functionally changes calcium handling through matrix Gla protein and osteocalcin | Vascular stiffness and calcification hypotheses | Small surrogate studies | Does not constitute a validated plasma-calcium intervention; warfarin interaction |
| Local metal-release biomaterials | Raises or redistributes metal ions locally in tissue | Angiogenesis, myocardial repair, ischemia–reperfusion injury | Preclinical | No human plasma target or cardiovascular-event evidence |

### Supplementation and repletion

Supplementation is the most familiar form of metal modulation. It can raise intake, correct a measurable deficiency, or alter a functional biomarker. However, the same dose may have different effects depending on baseline status, formulation, renal function, diet, medications, and the compartment being measured.

A person with severe magnesium deficiency, iron-deficient heart failure, or selenium deficiency associated with parenteral nutrition is not equivalent to a replete person seeking cardiovascular optimization. The former may benefit because a physiological bottleneck is being corrected. The latter is being exposed to a pharmacological perturbation without a proven therapeutic deficit.

Potassium deserves a related but separate position. It is an essential metal cation and dietary potassium is associated with blood-pressure and cardiovascular outcomes, but plasma potassium is tightly regulated and can become dangerous when renal excretion is impaired or medications interfere. The supplied genetic evidence concerns dietary intake rather than a validated plasma-potassium target, and it does not establish a cardiovascular supplementation regimen.

### Chelation and binding

EDTA forms complexes with divalent and trivalent ions and promotes urinary excretion. The 2002 stable-angina trial described affinity for lead, magnesium, zinc, iron, and calcium. This broad binding profile is central to both the proposed mechanism and the safety concern: a treatment intended to lower a toxic metal may also remove essential ions ([stable-angina EDTA trial](https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama/fullarticle/321724)).

Toxicology chelators are more targeted than EDTA, but none should be conceptualized as a general cardiovascular “detoxification” therapy. Succimer, or DMSA, is an oral chelator used particularly for lead and selected mercury or arsenic exposures. DMPS is used in some countries for inorganic mercury and arsenic but is not FDA-approved in the United States. Dimercaprol is an intramuscular agent reserved for selected severe poisonings. Alpha-lipoic acid, dihydrolipoic acid, cysteine, and glutathione have metal-binding or redox properties, but they are not established substitutes for clinically indicated chelation ([heavy-metal clinical management review](https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/27/8/3513)).

The distinction between toxicology chelation and cardiovascular chelation is decisive. In acute lead encephalopathy or severe inorganic arsenic poisoning, rapid removal can be life-saving. In stable coronary disease with modest environmental exposure, lowering a biomarker does not establish that cardiovascular risk will fall.

### Removing iron

Iron can be lowered by phlebotomy or iron-reduction strategies, but lowering iron is not automatically beneficial. FeAST tested defined-volume phlebotomy in stable symptomatic peripheral arterial disease while avoiding iron deficiency. It did not significantly reduce mortality or the composite of death, nonfatal myocardial infarction, and stroke.

Conversely, intravenous iron raises iron availability in patients with heart failure and iron deficiency. The clinical question is not whether plasma iron should be maximized, but whether a specific iron-deficient heart-failure phenotype should receive repletion based on hemoglobin, ferritin, and transferrin saturation.

### Functional redistribution rather than concentration lowering

Vitamin K is an adjacent intervention because it may change calcium handling without lowering plasma calcium. Vitamin K-dependent carboxylation activates matrix Gla protein, which can inhibit vascular calcification, and activates osteocalcin, which participates in bone calcium handling. Small trials reported preserved vascular elasticity with vitamin K1 and reduced pulse-wave velocity with menaquinone-7, but neither study measured cardiovascular events or established a plasma-calcium target ([vitamin K review](https://doi.org/10.3390/biomedicines11123154)).

Similarly, local hydrogels and scaffolds can release magnesium or strontium directly into injured myocardium. A magnesium-containing hydrogel released magnesium for more than 15 days and promoted angiogenesis in experimental models; a strontium-containing hydrogel reduced cardiomyocyte apoptosis and increased angiogenesis in a murine ischemia–reperfusion model. These are local tissue-engineering strategies, not systemic plasma-ion therapies, and they remain preclinical ([metal-ion biomaterials review](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10761210/)).

## 3. Supplementation and preventive cardiovascular outcomes

### Magnesium: reliable biomarker engagement, incomplete clinical proof

Magnesium is the best-developed candidate among the essential mineral supplements, but its clinical evidence is still divided between deficiency treatment, risk-factor improvement, perioperative arrhythmia prevention, and long-term cardiovascular prevention.

A meta-analysis of 48 randomized trials involving 2,131 adults found that oral magnesium doses ranged from 197 to 994 mg of elemental magnesium per day, with durations from 3 weeks to 5 years and a median duration of 12 weeks. Compared with placebo, circulating magnesium increased by 0.04 mmol/L and 24-hour urinary magnesium excretion increased by 1.52 mmol/24 hours. Circulating magnesium approached a pharmacodynamic plateau at approximately 300 mg/day after about 20 weeks, while urinary magnesium reached a plateau at approximately 400 mg/day after about 40 weeks. These are biomarker kinetics, not cardiovascular treatment targets ([magnesium biomarker meta-analysis](https://scholarworks.indianapolis.iu.edu/bitstreams/c209a949-b974-43ad-b004-ae59140dc35d/download)).

Baseline status modified the response. When baseline circulating magnesium was at least 0.87 mmol/L, supplementation produced little or no further circulating increase but increased urinary excretion. This supports targeting deficiency or likely depletion rather than supplementing everyone to achieve a higher number.

Randomized blood-pressure evidence is more encouraging than event evidence. A 34-trial meta-analysis involving 2,028 adults used a median of 368 mg/day for 3 months and found a 0.05 mmol/L serum-magnesium increase, a 2.00 mm Hg reduction in systolic blood pressure, and a 1.78 mm Hg reduction in diastolic blood pressure. A newer synthesis of 38 trials involving 2,709 adults found reductions of 2.81 and 2.05 mm Hg, respectively, but heterogeneity was high and there was no significant linear or nonlinear dose-response relationship ([2016 blood-pressure meta-analysis](https://www.ahajournals.org/doi/full/10.1161/hypertensionaha.116.07664); [2025 magnesium meta-analysis](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12529988/)).

The subgroup signal is clinically plausible but not definitive. In the 2025 synthesis, hypertensive participants already taking blood-pressure medication had estimated systolic and diastolic reductions of 7.68 and 2.96 mm Hg, while people with hypomagnesemia had reductions of 5.97 and 4.75 mm Hg. These analyses involved only six and eight trials, respectively, and did not demonstrate fewer cardiovascular events. Magnesium chloride appeared to produce larger blood-pressure effects, but every chloride study enrolled people with hypomagnesemia, so formulation and baseline deficiency were confounded.

#### Named magnesium trials

| Named regimen | Population, formulation, dose, and duration | Concentration engagement or target | Cardiovascular outcome | Safety and limits |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| NCT02837328 | 59 adults older than 55 years without prior CVD; magnesium oxide 400 mg/day for 10 weeks | Ionized magnesium increased 0.03 mmol/L; total magnesium increased 0.04 mmol/L; no target was established | Designed for primary prevention of supraventricular arrhythmia; reported findings did not show reduced arrhythmias or events | Ionized magnesium required specialized testing and had no validated long-term threshold |
| MAGiCAL-CKD | 148 adults with predialysis CKD, eGFR 15–45; magnesium hydroxide 15 mmol twice daily for 12 months | Plasma magnesium 0.94 versus 0.82 mmol/L; a prior open-label study proposed 1.04–1.25 mmol/L but achieved 0.88 mmol/L | Coronary-artery-calcification difference 0.9% (95% CI −10.2% to 13.4%; P=.438) | Diarrhea or loose stool 47% versus 12%; intensive monitoring; safety-event counts were small and hypothesis-generating |
| NCT02966912 | 40 adults with obesity and no clinical HF; magnesium oxide 400 mg twice daily for 24 weeks | No target or results posted in the supplied registry evidence | MRI and vascular-surrogate outcomes planned; no clinical event result available | Completed registry record, but no posted results; CKD and established CVD were excluded |
| Cardiac-surgery magnesium trials | 24 RCTs, 3,373 adults without prior AF; mostly intravenous magnesium, only two oral studies | Regimens and achieved plasma targets varied | Postoperative AF RR 0.55 (95% CI 0.41–0.74), low certainty; lower-risk studies RR 0.70 (0.58–0.84) | Mortality RR 1.00 (0.34–2.90); caution in severe renal impairment or hemodynamic instability |

MAGiCAL-CKD is especially instructive because it achieved clear plasma-magnesium separation without slowing coronary calcification. The trial enrolled 148 participants rather than the planned 250 because of slow recruitment. Magnesium adherence was high—97% took more than 95% of study medication under pill-count monitoring—but 11% reduced the dose and 4% discontinued because of gastrointestinal symptoms. The Results section reported six major adverse cardiovascular events in the magnesium group and none in placebo, although the study was not powered for this endpoint and the abstract and Results section differed on the number of deaths. This is a safety signal requiring caution, not proof that magnesium caused harm ([MAGiCAL-CKD](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10125639/)).

Magnesium is therefore feasible when used for a defined indication, but routine supplementation to prevent atherosclerotic events remains unproven. A 2025 ambulatory-care guideline proposes considering supplementation below 0.9 mmol/L and regards it as necessary at or below 0.8 mmol/L, with 600 mg/day for repletion, 350 mg/day for prevention, treatment for at least 3 months, and a proposed maintenance range of 0.85–0.95 mmol/L. These recommendations address magnesium deficiency management, not a validated cardiovascular target, and should not be interpreted as evidence that raising serum magnesium above the normal range prevents coronary disease ([2025 magnesium guideline](https://www.mdpi.com/2072-6643/17/5/887)).

### Calcium: uncertain safety and no cardiovascular benefit

Calcium supplementation illustrates why a normal or desirable skeletal nutrient is not automatically a cardiovascular therapy. Calcium is essential for contraction, coagulation, and vascular signaling, but supplementation can produce transient changes in serum calcium and may interact with vascular calcification or thrombosis pathways.

Bolland and colleagues’ 2010 patient-level meta-analysis included five randomized placebo-controlled trials involving 8,151 participants receiving at least 500 mg/day of calcium without coadministered vitamin D. Over a median 3.6 years, myocardial infarction occurred in 143 calcium recipients versus 111 placebo recipients, with a hazard ratio of 1.31 (95% CI 1.02–1.67). A trial-level analysis of 11 studies involving 11,921 participants found a pooled myocardial-infarction relative risk of 1.27 (1.01–1.59), while stroke, composite events, and death were not statistically significant ([Bolland calcium meta-analysis](https://www.bmj.com/content/341/bmj.c3691)).

Later evidence weakened but did not eliminate concern. Huo and colleagues’ analysis of seven calcium-alone comparisons involving 8,634 participants found no statistically significant excess myocardial-infarction risk: RR 1.15 (0.88–1.51). Six calcium-plus-vitamin-D trials involving 46,804 participants also found no significant excess risk, with an MI RR of 1.09 (0.95–1.25). However, none of the trials had cardiovascular disease as a primary endpoint, and event counts were insufficient to exclude a small but clinically important hazard ([updated calcium meta-analysis](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10111600/)).

The Women’s Health Initiative produced a further complicating signal. Among women not already taking personal calcium, 1 g/day of calcium plus 400 IU/day of vitamin D was associated with a clinical MI hazard ratio of 1.22 (95% CI 1.00–1.50). The authors acknowledged that subgroup analysis could compromise the balancing effect of randomization because calcium users and nonusers differed in baseline risk factors ([WHI calcium reanalysis](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3079822/)).

Genetic evidence points in the same direction as the concern but is not decisive. A Mendelian-randomization analysis found that a 1-standard-deviation, approximately 0.12 mmol/L, higher genetically predicted plasma calcium was associated with coronary heart disease, OR 1.25 (1.08–1.45), but horizontal pleiotropy could not be excluded. Lifelong genetically influenced calcium status is not equivalent to intermittent post-supplement serum-calcium excursions.

The practical judgment is not that calcium should be withheld when clinically indicated for bone health or deficiency. It is that calcium supplementation should not be prescribed as a cardiovascular preventive or therapeutic intervention, particularly when dietary adequacy is already present.

### Selenium: deficiency correction is plausible, universal prevention is unsupported

Selenium has one of the clearest U-shaped biological relationships. Severe deficiency can cause cardiomyopathy, including Keshan disease in selenium-poor regions, while excessive exposure can produce toxicity or adverse metabolic effects. This supports correction of deficiency but argues against indiscriminate supplementation.

A Cochrane review of 12 selenium-only randomized trials involving 19,715 participants found no statistically significant reduction in all-cause mortality, cardiovascular mortality, nonfatal cardiovascular events, or all cardiovascular events. Doses ranged from 100 to 800 μg/day and follow-up from weeks to 7–12 years. The pooled relative risks were 0.97 for all-cause mortality, 0.97 for cardiovascular mortality, 0.96 for nonfatal events, and 1.03 for all events ([selenium Cochrane review](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7433291/)).

Safety was not entirely neutral. Selenium supplementation showed a small, nonsignificant increase in type 2 diabetes overall, while SELECT reported increased alopecia and grade 1–2 dermatitis. A post hoc analysis of the Nutritional Prevention of Cancer trial associated 200 μg/day of selenium yeast with type 2 diabetes, particularly among men and participants with high baseline plasma selenium; the highest tertile, above 121.6 ng/mL, had a hazard ratio of 2.70. These findings do not define a cardiovascular toxicity threshold, but they reinforce the narrow therapeutic window.

A 43-trial systematic review with supplementation lasting at least 24 weeks also found no association between selenium alone and cardiovascular disease, cardiovascular mortality, cancer, cancer mortality, or all-cause mortality. The evidence certainty for selenium-only supplementation was low because event rates were low and cardiovascular outcomes were often secondary ([selenium randomized-trial meta-analysis](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7727482/)).

One positive-looking study requires careful qualification. In a Swedish randomized trial, 443 adults aged 69–88 years with baseline serum selenium of approximately 67.7 μg/L received organic selenium yeast 200 μg/day plus coenzyme Q10 200 mg/day or placebo for 48 months, followed by six years without active treatment. At 10 years, cardiovascular mortality was 11.3% versus 33.0% among women and 29.6% versus 44.5% among men; reported hazard ratios were 0.29 and 0.61, respectively. The intervention also improved inflammatory, oxidative-stress, natriuretic-peptide, and renal-function markers ([Swedish selenium–coenzyme Q10 trial](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-3921/14/6/685)).

This is important evidence for a low-selenium, elderly subgroup, but it cannot establish selenium monotherapy. The trial used selenium and coenzyme Q10 together, involved a narrow Swedish population, was retrospectively registered, and included a relatively small number of events. Its findings should be treated as a subgroup signal requiring independent replication, not as justification for universal selenium supplementation.

Clinical laboratory practice also illustrates the distinction between deficiency treatment and cardiovascular optimization. One laboratory source describes raising serum selenium above 70 μg/L in selenium deficiency associated with total parenteral nutrition and recommends semiannual monitoring. Another reference interval for adults is 110–165 μg/L. These values are not interchangeable therapeutic targets, and neither is validated for cardiovascular prevention ([selenium laboratory guidance](https://essentiahealth.testcatalog.org/show/LAB1589)).

### Zinc: metabolic and surrogate signals without event evidence

Zinc is essential for transcription, immune function, antioxidant enzymes, glucose metabolism, and vascular signaling. Its relationship with cardiovascular disease is plausibly nonlinear: deficiency may impair endothelial and immune function, while excess can cause copper deficiency, anemia, renal injury, and oxidative stress.

A systematic review of 27 publications comprising 34 datasets included 1,042 zinc-treated and 974 control participants. Elemental zinc doses ranged from 9.8 to 75 mg/day for 4 weeks to 12 months. Effects varied by dose and duration, but reported benefits were mainly changes in fasting glucose, insulin resistance, triglycerides, total cholesterol, and LDL cholesterol. No cardiovascular-event reduction or validated plasma-zinc target was established ([zinc supplementation review](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7850144/)).

A separate meta-analysis of 20 trials involving 1,141 zinc-treated participants found reductions in triglycerides, VLDL, total cholesterol, fasting glucose, and HbA1c, but not blood pressure. Again, these were risk-factor outcomes rather than cardiovascular events ([zinc meta-analysis](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31494808/)).

Small post-MI studies do not close the evidence gap. In a randomized trial of 50 patients with acute MI after PCI, polaprezinc increased blood and urine zinc, lowered an IL-6/maximal-creatine-phosphokinase ratio, and was associated with improved ejection fraction over follow-up. The supplied report did not provide a recurrent-event endpoint, a cardiovascular mortality result, a zinc target, or complete safety data ([polaprezinc post-MI trial](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30855449/)).

A proposed diabetes trial of zinc gluconate 30 mg/day for 4 months was withdrawn with actual enrollment of zero and no results. Its planned endpoints were pulse-wave velocity, cerebrovascular reactivity, exercise blood-pressure response, and platelet aggregation, not clinical events ([NCT05000762](https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05000762)). High-dose zinc should therefore be reserved for a documented indication and monitored for copper depletion rather than used as cardiovascular prevention.

### Copper: biochemical response without clinical efficacy

Copper supports mitochondrial respiration, iron metabolism, connective tissue, and copper–zinc superoxide dismutase. Both deficiency and excess can damage the cardiovascular system, but no clinically validated strategy deliberately raises plasma copper to prevent cardiovascular disease.

A randomized trial in healthy middle-aged adults with moderately high cholesterol tested copper glycinate 2 mg/day for 8 weeks. Copper increased erythrocyte superoxide dismutase 1 and plasma ceruloplasmin, but did not significantly change C-reactive protein, homocysteine, or total, LDL, or HDL cholesterol. Oxidized LDL fell inconsistently. A 2021 meta-analysis of five copper trials involving only 176 participants found no significant effect on total cholesterol, LDL cholesterol, or HDL cholesterol ([copper supplementation trial](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22444781/); [copper meta-analysis](https://doi.org/10.1007/s12011-020-02423-1)).

Copper measurement is also biologically complicated because most circulating copper is protein-bound, especially to ceruloplasmin. Serum copper may rise with inflammation without reflecting increased biologically active copper. The supplied evidence does not establish a cardiovascular target concentration, an event benefit, or a complete safety and interaction profile. Correcting documented deficiency is clinically different from raising copper in a replete patient.

### High-dose multivitamins and minerals

The most direct test of a broad metal-supplement strategy was the vitamin component of TACT. The active regimen contained six caplets daily and supplied calcium 500 mg, magnesium 500 mg, zinc 20 mg, copper 2 mg, selenium 200 μg, potassium 99 mg, manganese 20 mg, chromium 200 μg, molybdenum 150 μg, iodine 150 μg, boron 2 mg, and vanadium 39 μg, together with high doses of several vitamins. No prespecified plasma concentration target was reported, and the study did not demonstrate that the formulation changed plasma metal status in a clinically relevant way ([TACT multivitamin trial](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4143134/)).

Among 1,708 stable post-MI patients, the primary composite occurred in 230 of 853 active-treatment participants and 253 of 855 placebo participants: HR 0.89 (95% CI 0.75–1.07; P=.21). The cardiovascular-death, MI, or stroke composite was also nonsignificant, HR 0.82 (0.62–1.07; P=.142). Serious adverse events occurred in 15% versus 12%.

Almost 46% discontinued the assigned vitamin regimen, and median exposure was 31 months in the active group versus 35 months in placebo. The regimen therefore demonstrated that long-term administration is possible in selected trial participants, but adherence was a major limitation. The result does not support replacing statins, antiplatelet therapy, or other evidence-based secondary prevention with high-dose multivitamins.

### Vitamin K and the calcium-handling hypothesis

Vitamin K is not a metal supplement, but it has been proposed as a way to alter calcium distribution rather than serum calcium itself. In a study of 121 healthy participants, vitamin K1 100 μg/day for 3 years maintained vascular elasticity while placebo participants experienced a reported 12% loss. In 244 postmenopausal women, menaquinone-7 180 μg/day for 3 years reduced pulse-wave velocity. Both were surrogate outcomes; neither established fewer cardiovascular events.

Observational studies of vitamin K2 intake and cardiovascular disease have been inconsistent, and associations weakened after dietary-confounder adjustment. Vitamin K supplementation is also context-dependent: warfarin interferes with the vitamin K cycle, and ezetimibe can reduce intestinal vitamin K uptake. These considerations make vitamin K a research candidate for calcification biology, not a proven cardiovascular metal-modulation therapy.

### Overall preventive judgment

For primary prevention, the evidence supports adequate nutrition and correction of true deficiencies, not pharmacological optimization of plasma metal concentrations. A U.S. Preventive Services Task Force evidence review of 84 studies involving 739,803 participants found little or no benefit from vitamin and mineral supplementation for preventing cardiovascular disease or death, while evidence for magnesium, selenium, and zinc was low, insufficient, or absent ([USPSTF evidence review](https://www.uspreventiveservicestaskforce.org/home/getfilebytoken/U4Vu9hcmHtD7snox6qbPja)).

For secondary prevention after MI, TACT’s high-dose multivitamin/mineral regimen was neutral and adherence was poor. The selenium–coenzyme Q10 trial provides a potentially important low-selenium signal, but its combination design and narrow population prevent broad application. For most patients, dietary adequacy and standard cardiovascular prevention remain better supported than deliberate elevation of plasma zinc, copper, selenium, calcium, or magnesium.

## 4. Chelation, iron reduction, and other interventions in established disease

### TACT: an isolated positive chelation signal

TACT was a double-blind, placebo-controlled, 2×2 factorial trial conducted from 2003 to 2011 and published in 2013. It enrolled 1,708 adults aged 50 years or older who had experienced an MI at least six weeks earlier. Participants received 40 infusions of a 500 mL solution containing 3 g disodium EDTA, 7 g ascorbate, B vitamins, electrolytes, procaine, and heparin, or matching placebo. Infusions were weekly for 30 weeks, followed by 10 infusions given 2–8 weeks apart.

Over a median 55-month follow-up, the primary composite of death, recurrent MI, stroke, coronary revascularization, or hospitalization for angina occurred in 222 of 839 chelation participants (26%) and 261 of 869 placebo participants (30%). The hazard ratio was 0.82 (95% CI 0.69–0.99; P=.035). Total mortality was not reduced: 87 deaths (10%) versus 93 (11%), HR 0.93 (0.70–1.25; P=.64).

The result was modest and driven substantially by revascularization rather than mortality. Infusion discontinuation because of adverse events occurred in 16% of the EDTA group and 15% of placebo. The investigators concluded that the findings were not sufficient to support routine chelation after MI.

TACT was biologically intriguing because EDTA binds multiple ions, including lead and calcium, and may also influence iron stores, oxidative stress, vascular tone, or plaque biology. It was not a lead-specific intervention, however. The trial could not determine whether any benefit arose from lead removal, removal of another metal, non-chelation ingredients, altered calcium handling, or chance.

### TACT2: biomarker success without cardiovascular benefit

TACT2 was designed to replicate TACT in a subgroup thought to have benefited most: adults aged 50 years or older with diabetes and previous MI. The trial enrolled 1,000 participants, of whom 959 received at least one assigned infusion. It was a double-masked 2×2 factorial trial at 88 U.S. and Canadian sites. Participants were scheduled for 40 weekly 500 mL infusions containing up to 3 g EDTA adjusted for renal function, or placebo, alongside a twice-daily oral high-dose multivitamin/mineral or placebo for 60 months.

| Trial | Population and intervention | Primary cardiovascular result | Metal-status result | Current interpretation |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| TACT | 1,708 adults ≥50 years, prior MI; 40 EDTA or placebo infusions | Composite 26% vs 30%; HR 0.82 (0.69–0.99); mortality neutral | Multi-metal intervention; no validated plasma target | Positive but modest, not sufficient for routine use |
| TACT vitamins | Same factorial population; six caplets/day of 28-component formula | 230/853 vs 253/855; HR 0.89 (0.75–1.07; P=.21) | No measured plasma-metal target reported | No significant secondary-prevention benefit |
| TACT2 | 959 adults with diabetes and prior MI; 40 EDTA or placebo infusions | 35.6% vs 35.7%; adjusted HR 0.93 (0.76–1.16; P=.53) | Blood lead fell from 9.03 to 3.46 μg/L; placebo 9.3 to 8.7 μg/L | Biomarker reduction did not translate into event reduction |
| IRONMAN | 1,137 adults with symptomatic HF, LVEF ≤45%, and iron deficiency; ferric derisomaltose | 904 vs 1,086 unplanned hospitalizations; rate ratio 0.83 (0.71–0.97) in later recurrent-event analysis | Redosing based on ferritin and TSAT, not plasma iron | Supports selected IV-iron treatment, with endpoint and mortality uncertainty |
| FeAST | 1,277 patients with stable symptomatic PAD; six-monthly phlebotomy | Mortality HR 0.85 (0.67–1.08); death/MI/stroke HR 0.88 (0.72–1.07) | Iron stores reduced without iron deficiency | No support for routine iron depletion |

Over a median 48 months, the TACT2 primary composite occurred in 172 of 483 EDTA participants (35.6%) and 170 of 476 placebo participants (35.7%). The adjusted HR was 0.93 (95% CI 0.76–1.16; P=.53). Cardiovascular death, MI, or stroke occurred in 18.4% versus 19.7%, HR 0.89 (0.66–1.19), and all-cause mortality was 17.4% versus 17.6%, HR 0.96 (0.71–1.30) ([TACT2 randomized trial](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11325247/)).

The intervention clearly engaged one proposed toxic-metal mechanism. Median blood lead fell from 9.0 to 3.5 μg/L by infusion 40, a 61% reduction. Placebo changed from 9.3 to 8.7 μg/L. Urine cadmium did not show a clinically relevant end-of-study reduction, although it rose transiently after infusion. TACT2 therefore provides unusually strong evidence that a biomarker can improve without a corresponding cardiovascular benefit.

Only 68% of active-chelation participants completed all 40 infusions, although 78% received at least 20. Serious adverse events were similar in the EDTA and placebo groups, 16.8% and 16.6%, respectively. Eligibility excluded creatinine above 2.0 mg/dL, recent smoking, recent heart-failure hospitalization, uncontrolled blood pressure, and inability to tolerate weekly 500 mL infusions, so feasibility is bounded to a relatively selected population.

The reasons for the difference between TACT and TACT2 remain uncertain. TACT2 participants may have had more advanced coronary disease but lower lead exposure, and they received more contemporary background therapy, including statins, antiplatelet agents, sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors, and glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists. These are plausible contextual explanations, not demonstrated effect modifiers ([ACC TACT2 interpretation](https://www.acc.org/latest-in-cardiology/clinical-trials/2024/04/05/04/40/tact2)).

The TACT2 paper reported the infusion comparison. In the supplied evidence, the cardiovascular and plasma-concentration results of the separate TACT2 high-dose multivitamin/mineral component remain unavailable. The oral supplement was assigned twice daily for 60 months, but its outcome cannot be inferred from the EDTA result.

### Broader chelation evidence

The Cochrane review updated through August 2019 included five randomized studies involving 1,993 participants and rated the evidence generally low or very low certainty. For coronary disease, chelation showed no clear effect on all-cause mortality, RR 0.97 (95% CI 0.73–1.28), or MI, RR 0.81 (0.57–1.14). Stroke was also not clearly reduced, RR 0.88 (0.40–1.92). In peripheral vascular disease, chelation did not improve ankle–brachial index or maximum or pain-free walking distance; the one positive ankle–brachial study had high risk of bias ([Cochrane chelation review](https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD002785_chelation-therapy-atherosclerotic-cardiovascular-heart-and-circulation-disease)).

An earlier randomized placebo-controlled trial of 84 patients with stable angina and treadmill ischemia gave 33 EDTA treatments and found no improvement in exercise capacity or patient-perceived well-being over one year. It was not powered for clinical events. One participant had a reversible creatinine rise from 1.5 to 2.1 mg/dL during the first 10 treatments, illustrating why renal monitoring matters.

Taken together, TACT remains a clinically interesting positive trial, but TACT2 and the broader randomized evidence do not support EDTA chelation as routine secondary prevention. A reduction in blood lead or urinary metal excretion is not sufficient evidence of cardiovascular efficacy.

### Iron depletion: FeAST and the iron hypothesis

The FeAST trial tested whether lowering iron stores would reduce cardiovascular events in 1,277 patients with symptomatic but stable peripheral arterial disease. Participants were randomized to defined-volume phlebotomy every six months while avoiding iron deficiency or to usual care. All-cause mortality was 23% in control versus 20% with phlebotomy, HR 0.85 (95% CI 0.67–1.08; P=.17). Death plus nonfatal MI or stroke was 32% versus 28%, HR 0.88 (0.72–1.07; P=.20). Neither endpoint was significantly improved ([FeAST trial](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17299195/)).

Phlebotomy therefore does not support routine iron-store depletion for secondary prevention in stable PAD. It also illustrates that a plausible oxidative-stress mechanism may not translate into a benefit when the intervention changes a broad physiological system rather than correcting a specific deficiency.

Iron removal can affect other metals. A review reports that phlebotomy in hemochromatosis has increased cadmium and lead levels and altered trace-element concentrations in some anemia settings. This collateral effect reinforces the need to distinguish iron overload treatment from cardiovascular prevention.

### Intravenous iron in heart failure

Iron deficiency is common in heart failure and can impair erythropoiesis, skeletal-muscle metabolism, mitochondrial function, and myocardial energetics even when anemia is absent. The clinical question is therefore whether iron repletion improves a defined heart-failure phenotype, not whether increasing plasma iron benefits the general population.

The strongest therapeutic signal comes from pooled randomized evidence. A 2025 individual-participant and trial-level meta-analysis included FAIR-HF, CONFIRM-HF, AFFIRM-AHF, IRONMAN, HEART-FID, and FAIR-HF2: six multicenter trials involving 7,175 patients with heart failure, iron deficiency, and LVEF ≤50%. Five trials used ferric carboxymaltose and IRONMAN used ferric derisomaltose.

Compared with control, intravenous iron reduced the composite of recurrent heart-failure hospitalizations and cardiovascular death at 12 months, RR 0.72 (95% CI 0.55–0.89), and over complete follow-up, RR 0.81 (0.63–0.97). Recurrent heart-failure hospitalization alone at 12 months had an RR of 0.69 (0.48–0.88). Cardiovascular mortality alone was directionally lower but not statistically definitive, HR 0.80 (0.61–1.03), and all-cause mortality was similarly uncertain. Infection and serious adverse-event rates were similar between groups ([2025 intravenous-iron meta-analysis](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41591-025-03671-1)).

The pooled result is clinically meaningful but not conclusive. Treatment effects were greatest in the first year, when average exposure was approximately 2,000 mg, compared with 300–900 mg per year in years 2 and 3. Maintenance dosing was often less than intended, and the optimal schedule remains unresolved. No statistically significant interaction was found by age, ischemic etiology, NYHA class, eGFR, hemoglobin, ferritin, or transferrin saturation. An apparent sex interaction suggested no benefit among women, but the authors cautioned that it might reflect chance or confounding and it was inconsistent across trials.

#### HEART-FID

HEART-FID enrolled 3,065 ambulatory adults with heart failure, LVEF ≤40%, iron deficiency, and specified hemoglobin criteria. Ferric carboxymaltose was given in two doses seven days apart, followed by repeat dosing every six months as needed according to hemoglobin and iron indices. At 12 months, death occurred in 8.6% versus 10.3%, and heart-failure hospitalizations were 297 versus 332, but the prespecified hierarchical primary outcome was neutral at its stringent significance threshold: win ratio 1.10, 99% CI 0.99–1.23, with P=.02 against a prespecified threshold of .01.

Serious adverse events were similar, 27.0% versus 26.2%. HEART-FID therefore supports protocol feasibility and a possible hospitalization signal, but not a definitive mortality or hierarchical-outcome benefit ([HEART-FID report](https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa2304968)).

#### AFFIRM-AHF and IRONMAN

AFFIRM-AHF randomized 1,132 patients hospitalized with acute heart failure, LVEF below 50%, and iron deficiency to ferric carboxymaltose or placebo. The rate ratio for cardiovascular death plus total heart-failure hospitalizations was 0.79 (95% CI 0.62–1.01; P=.059). The original IRONMAN comparison produced a similar rate ratio of 0.82 (0.66–1.02; P=.070), narrowly missing its primary endpoint.

A later IRONMAN analysis examined recurrent all-cause hospitalizations over a median 2.7 years in 1,137 participants with symptomatic heart failure, LVEF ≤45%, and transferrin saturation below 20% or ferritin below 100 μg/L. Ferric derisomaltose recipients experienced 904 unplanned all-cause hospitalization events compared with 1,086 under usual care, rate ratio 0.83 (95% CI 0.71–0.97; P=.02). Cardiovascular and noncardiovascular hospitalization rate ratios were each 0.83, but the cause-specific analyses were descriptive and the trial was not powered to establish mortality differences ([IRONMAN extended analysis](https://www.jacc.org/doi/10.1016/j.jacc.2024.08.052)).

The IRONMAN protocol permitted up to 20 mg/kg of ferric derisomaltose, with a maximum of 2,000 mg per infusion. Participants were reviewed at four weeks and every four months. Repeat dosing was requested when ferritin was below 100 μg/L or, if ferritin was no higher than 400 μg/L, transferrin saturation was below 25%. The trial did not specify a target plasma iron concentration.

A 2024 biomarker analysis suggested greater event rates and potentially greater absolute benefit among patients with anemia or transferrin saturation below 20%, especially when ferritin was at least 100 μg/L. The subgroup findings were not statistically definitive and were explicitly described as hypothesis-generating ([IRONMAN biomarker analysis](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38446126/)).

A 2026 Canadian health-technology review reached a more cautious conclusion. It found limited short-term quality-of-life improvement and no clear effect on mortality, hospitalization, or exercise capacity versus usual care for ferric derisomaltose. A cardiovascular-death or hospitalization composite appeared less frequent, but the evidence was uncertain because of imprecision and risk of bias. The review found no adult head-to-head evidence comparing ferric derisomaltose with ferric carboxymaltose or other intravenous products ([2026 ferric-derisomaltose review](https://doi.org/10.51731/cjht.2026.1356)).

The resulting judgment is that intravenous iron is the most credible therapeutic metal-status intervention for cardiovascular disease, but its support is indication-specific and endpoint-specific. It is reasonable to consider in patients with symptomatic heart failure and guideline-defined iron deficiency; it is not evidence for indiscriminate iron elevation or for treating coronary disease without iron deficiency.

### Oral iron

Oral iron is a supplementation strategy, but it has not reproduced the functional effects of intravenous iron in heart failure. IRONOUT HF found no improvement in exercise capacity among patients with HFrEF and iron deficiency, and guidelines do not recommend oral iron for that population. The supplied evidence does not provide a dose, duration, achieved plasma target, or cardiovascular-event result for IRONOUT HF. The contrast with intravenous iron may reflect absorption, inflammation, hepcidin-mediated sequestration, dose delivery, or disease severity, but it does not justify assuming that oral iron prevents cardiovascular events.

## 5. Feasibility, safety, monitoring, and clinical guidance

### Monitoring must follow the intervention

There is no single “metal panel” that can guide cardiovascular treatment. The correct assay depends on the metal, its chemical form, the clinical question, and the intervention.

| Intervention | Appropriate monitoring | Target or trigger supported by the evidence | Principal safety issue | Practical status |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Magnesium replacement | Serum magnesium, renal function, symptoms; ionized magnesium only with validated specimen handling | One guideline proposes considering treatment below 0.9 mmol/L and maintaining 0.85–0.95 mmol/L; not a CVD target | Diarrhea, hypermagnesemia in renal impairment, medication and diuretic effects | Oral products widely available; clinical target remains deficiency-oriented |
| Intravenous iron | Hemoglobin, ferritin, transferrin saturation, heart-failure status, repeat dosing history | Trial eligibility and redosing used ferritin and TSAT; no plasma-iron target | Misclassification of deficiency, repeated infusion burden, uncertain long-term maintenance | Available for selected heart-failure patients |
| Selenium | Serum or plasma selenium using a validated assay; functional markers may help in research | >70 μg/L is described for parenteral-nutrition deficiency; reference intervals vary; no CVD target | Narrow therapeutic window, possible diabetes and dermatologic signals | Deficiency testing and replacement available; cardiovascular use unproven |
| Zinc and copper | Serum or plasma zinc and copper, with attention to albumin, inflammation, and nutrient interactions | No validated cardiovascular concentration or treatment threshold | High zinc can cause copper deficiency; excess copper can promote oxidative injury | Replacement feasible when deficiency is documented |
| Calcium and vitamin K | Serum calcium and indication-specific testing; vascular-stiffness measures remain research endpoints | No validated plasma-calcium target for CVD prevention | Possible calcium cardiovascular harm signal; warfarin interaction with vitamin K | Routine products available, but not as CVD therapy |
| Lead, cadmium, mercury, arsenic | Venous blood lead; creatinine-adjusted urine cadmium; species-specific blood or urine mercury; urine arsenic speciation | Toxicology action thresholds are not cardiovascular targets | Persistent body stores, matrix error, ongoing exposure, chelator toxicity | Testing available through specialized laboratories |
| EDTA or toxicology chelation | Renal function, calcium and electrolytes, CBC, hepatic status, clinical symptoms, serial appropriate metal biomarker | Chelation should follow species, symptoms, and validated toxicology thresholds | Hypocalcemia, kidney injury, loss of essential metals, hypersensitivity | EDTA for coronary disease is not FDA-approved and requires infusion infrastructure |

### Magnesium measurement is feasible but imperfect

The 2020 magnesium pilot used a point-of-care analyzer to measure normalized ionized magnesium in fresh whole blood. In 39 split specimens, refrigeration raised the measured serum ionized magnesium by 0.14 mmol/L compared with fresh whole blood, while one freeze–thaw cycle raised it by 0.20 mmol/L. Ionized magnesium is also sensitive to pH and serum calcium and lacks a threshold linked to long-term cardiovascular outcomes.

A 2025 guideline proposes rechecking serum magnesium after one month and then every three months during repletion. It lists nausea, vomiting, loose stool, and diarrhea as common adverse effects and suggests dividing the dose when symptoms are severe. The guideline also notes that renal function, antacids, proton-pump inhibitors, antibiotics, contraceptives, and diuretics can affect magnesium handling or absorption. These recommendations are useful for deficiency management but have not been validated in event-prevention trials.

### Iron monitoring is more clinically mature

Intravenous-iron trials used hemoglobin, ferritin, and transferrin saturation rather than plasma iron concentration. This reflects the biology of iron deficiency: plasma iron fluctuates substantially and is not a reliable standalone measure of tissue iron availability. Ferritin is useful but rises with inflammation, obesity, liver disease, kidney disease, alcohol use, and cancer. Spectrophotometric serum iron can vary by as much as 70% within an individual from day to day ([iron biomarkers review](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12011-024-04289-z)).

The practical consequence is that eligibility and retreatment should be based on the same indices used in the validated trials, with clinical context. A normal or elevated ferritin does not necessarily exclude functional deficiency, but neither does a low-normal transferrin saturation prove that intravenous iron will reduce events. The trial population and treatment indication matter.

### Trace-element testing does not establish therapeutic targets

Reference intervals are descriptive, not therapeutic. A 2025 Northern Spain study used inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry and Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute guidance to derive sex- and age-specific reference intervals for 27 elements in 501 healthy adults. It found sex and age differences in copper, mercury, iron, and other elements. Such intervals help laboratories interpret results, but they do not identify concentrations that prevent MI or stroke ([trace-element reference-interval study](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41043681/)).

For selenium, one laboratory lists an adult reference interval of 110–165 μg/L and warns that contrast media containing gadolinium, iodine, or barium can interfere with ICP-MS-based testing for up to 96 hours. Another source describes raising serum selenium above 70 μg/L for parenteral-nutrition deficiency. These values answer different questions and should not be merged into a cardiovascular target.

For zinc and copper, inflammation, albumin, ceruloplasmin, diet, and recent supplementation can alter the measurement. The evidence does not provide validated thresholds for intentionally raising or lowering either metal to prevent cardiovascular disease. For calcium, the body maintains plasma levels within a narrow range through parathyroid, renal, bone, and vitamin-D physiology; a normal calcium result does not exclude tissue calcium dysregulation, and increasing calcium intake is not equivalent to correcting hypocalcemia.

### Toxic-metal monitoring must be species- and matrix-specific

For lead, venous blood lead is the principal clinical test for recent exposure. It does not capture the full skeletal burden, which may be mobilized during pregnancy, lactation, osteoporosis, or endocrine disease. For cadmium, creatinine-corrected urine cadmium estimates body burden and should be interpreted with tubular-injury markers such as β2-microglobulin when renal toxicity is suspected.

For arsenic, total urine arsenic is uninterpretable without speciation because seafood-derived arsenobetaine can dominate the result without indicating toxic inorganic exposure. Patients should avoid seafood before testing, and laboratories should report inorganic arsenic, monomethylarsonic acid, and dimethylarsinic acid separately. For mercury, blood and hair are more useful for methylmercury exposure, while urine is more useful for inorganic mercury and renal exposure. These differences make an indiscriminate “plasma heavy-metal panel” clinically inadequate ([heavy-metal diagnostic review](https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/27/8/3513)).

Provoked urine testing after a chelator challenge is particularly problematic. It can increase urinary metal excretion pharmacologically and produce a misleading impression of body burden. Testing should be ordered only when the result will change exposure control, monitoring, or treatment.

### Adherence and delivery burden

Feasibility in a trial is not the same as feasibility in routine care.

In the magnesium CKD trial, 97% of participants took more than 95% of assigned tablets, but they received medication every 13 weeks, underwent fasting blood tests and 24-hour urine collections, and had pill counts. In TACT, 46% discontinued the vitamin regimen, which required six large caplets daily. In TACT2, only 68% of active-chelation participants completed all 40 infusions. In the selenium–coenzyme Q10 trial, returned medication was counted and there was no significant difference in unused medication between treatment groups.

Intravenous iron is less burdensome than 40 weekly EDTA infusions, but maintenance dosing is still difficult. The pooled intravenous-iron analysis found that most initial iron was delivered in the first 4–6 weeks and that later-year exposure was much lower than intended. This may explain why early heart-failure hospitalization effects are more consistent than long-term mortality effects.

Outside trials, complete data on cost, access, product quality, adherence, and long-term safety are unavailable for many oral metal regimens. Those missing fields should limit confidence rather than be filled with assumptions.

### Adverse effects and interactions

The main safety problem with metal modulation is that essentiality is not linear. Removing lead with EDTA may also increase urinary losses of calcium, magnesium, zinc, iron, and copper. The use of disodium EDTA rather than calcium disodium EDTA in the wrong clinical context can cause profound hypocalcemia. The National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health identifies hypocalcemia and kidney damage as the most important serious risks of EDTA chelation and notes that coronary chelation is not FDA-approved ([NCCIH chelation summary](https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/chelation-for-coronary-heart-disease-what-you-need-to-know)).

Magnesium commonly causes gastrointestinal symptoms and can accumulate in renal impairment. Intravenous magnesium requires caution in severe renal dysfunction and hemodynamic instability. Zinc can cause copper deficiency and iron-deficiency anemia when used excessively. Selenium has a narrow range in which functional benefit may be achieved, and long-term high-dose use has raised diabetes and dermatologic concerns. Calcium supplementation may carry cardiovascular risk in some populations even when it is appropriate for bone health.

Interactions are also metal-specific. Calcium and iron can compete for absorption and are often separated when both are prescribed. High zinc can deplete copper. Diuretics can increase magnesium losses. Warfarin interacts with vitamin K, and ezetimibe may affect vitamin K uptake. The supplied evidence does not provide a complete interaction or contraindication profile for every supplement, formulation, or exposure-reduction strategy.

### Practical clinical guidance

For a patient with a cardiovascular disease and a low metal value, the first question should be whether the result is valid and whether the deficiency is clinically meaningful. A repeat test, appropriate specimen, medication review, renal assessment, dietary history, and evaluation for gastrointestinal or renal losses may be more useful than automatically increasing the dose.

For iron-deficient heart failure, the best-supported pathway is to confirm the trial-like phenotype using hemoglobin, ferritin, and transferrin saturation, then consider intravenous iron within heart-failure care. Oral iron should not be assumed equivalent.

For magnesium, repletion is reasonable when deficiency is documented, when diuretic-associated losses are likely, or in selected perioperative settings. It should not be presented as proven prevention of coronary events. Renal function and gastrointestinal tolerance determine whether supplementation is safe.

For suspected toxic-metal exposure, source identification and reduction come first. Confirm the correct metal and species with the correct matrix. Chelation should be directed by a medical toxicologist and reserved for validated poisoning indications, significant symptoms, organ injury, or toxicology thresholds—not for nonspecific symptoms or an isolated unvalidated provoked result.

For calcium, zinc, selenium, copper, and high-dose multivitamins, routine cardiovascular prescribing is not supported. Deficiency replacement remains appropriate when the diagnosis is sound, but the cardiovascular claim should not be used to justify treatment.

## 6. Overall efficacy judgment, candidate populations, and evidence gaps

### Comparative evidence strength

| Intervention | Direction of modulation and setting | Main clinical endpoint | Evidence strength | Clinical judgment |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Intravenous iron in iron-deficient heart failure | Repletes iron availability using ferritin, TSAT, and hemoglobin criteria | Fewer recurrent HF hospitalizations; mortality uncertain | Moderate but heterogeneous pooled evidence; individual trials mixed | Credible therapy for selected symptomatic HF, not general iron optimization |
| Magnesium repletion or perioperative magnesium | Raises or restores magnesium; often intravenous perioperatively | Modest BP reduction; lower postoperative AF risk | Surrogate and low-to-moderate certainty event evidence; no long-term prevention proof | Use for deficiency and selected perioperative indications |
| Selenium plus CoQ10 in low-selenium elderly adults | Raises selenium and supplies a nonmetal antioxidant | Lower long-term CV mortality in one Swedish trial | Promising but low generalizability; selenium effect cannot be isolated | Hypothesis-generating subgroup signal, not universal supplementation |
| EDTA chelation after MI | Binds and removes multiple metals, including lead and calcium | TACT positive composite; TACT2 neutral | Conflicting RCTs; low-certainty pooled evidence | Do not use routinely for coronary disease |
| Phlebotomy in stable PAD | Lowers iron stores | No significant mortality or MI/stroke benefit | Well-conducted negative RCT | Not cardiovascular prevention |
| Calcium supplementation | Raises calcium intake, without a validated plasma target | No proven benefit; possible MI harm signal | Conflicting meta-analyses with limited event power | Do not prescribe for CVD prevention |
| Zinc or copper supplementation | Raises intake and sometimes circulating biomarkers | Metabolic or inflammatory surrogates only | Small, heterogeneous trials; no event evidence | Correct deficiency; no routine CVD use |
| Selenium-only supplementation | Raises selenium status | No general reduction in CVD events or mortality | Multiple randomized reviews largely null | Avoid universal use; treat severe deficiency |
| Toxic-metal source reduction | Lowers ongoing lead, cadmium, arsenic, or mercury exposure | Cardiovascular benefit inferred from exposure risk, not event RCTs | Strong epidemiological and public-health rationale; limited intervention evidence | High-priority prevention, especially in exposed communities |
| Toxicology chelation | Binds and removes specific toxic metals | Organ recovery in selected poisoning, not common CVD prevention | Established for selected poisonings; not for low-level CVD risk | Use only for validated toxicology indications |

### Which patients have credible support?

The most credible cardiovascular subgroup is the patient with symptomatic heart failure and confirmed iron deficiency. The benefit is most consistently expressed as fewer recurrent heart-failure hospitalizations, with uncertain effects on mortality. Treatment should be linked to the heart-failure phenotype and iron indices, not to an abstract desire to raise plasma iron.

A second, narrower group includes patients with documented magnesium deficiency, substantial renal or gastrointestinal magnesium loss, or diuretic-associated depletion. Magnesium replacement can correct a measurable physiological abnormality and may improve blood pressure or reduce postoperative atrial fibrillation. It has not been shown to prevent atherosclerotic events in generally replete adults.

A third possible subgroup consists of people with severe selenium deficiency, including those receiving long-term parenteral nutrition or living in severely selenium-deficient regions. Keshan disease demonstrates that profound selenium deficiency can be cardiomyopathic, but evidence from that deficiency extreme cannot be extrapolated to selenium-replete populations. The Swedish selenium–coenzyme Q10 trial identifies a possible low-selenium elderly subgroup, but the combination intervention and narrow setting prevent a general recommendation.

Patients with confirmed lead, arsenic, mercury, or other toxic-metal poisoning may benefit from source removal and, when indicated, species-specific chelation. This is treatment of poisoning, not evidence that lowering a modest environmental biomarker prevents coronary disease. For cadmium, chronic exposure reduction and renal protection are favored because chelation has limited benefit and may worsen renal toxicity.

### Which claims remain unsupported?

The evidence does not support routine use of oral magnesium, calcium, zinc, selenium, copper, potassium, or multivitamin/mineral mixtures to prevent MI, stroke, heart failure, or cardiovascular death in the general population. It does not support using a serum or plasma reference interval as a cardiovascular treatment target. It does not support substituting supplements or chelation for statins, antiplatelet therapy, blood-pressure treatment, diabetes treatment, smoking cessation, or exposure remediation.

The evidence also does not support transferring the TACT EDTA result to the TACT high-dose multivitamin regimen. TACT tested two factorial interventions, and the vitamin component was neutral. Nor can the Swedish selenium–coenzyme Q10 result be attributed to selenium alone.

Likewise, the failure of TACT2 does not prove that toxic-metal exposure is harmless. It shows that lowering blood lead through an EDTA regimen in stable post-MI patients with diabetes did not reduce cardiovascular events. Population exposure prevention may still be highly beneficial, especially because lead, cadmium, and arsenic affect multiple organs and are concentrated in communities with fewer resources to avoid exposure.

### What evidence would change the conclusion?

The field needs trials that begin with validated deficiency or exposure definitions, measure the relevant compartment, and use clinical endpoints. A study that randomizes patients with low magnesium, confirms intracellular or functional depletion, achieves a prespecified concentration range, and reduces cardiovascular events would provide stronger evidence than a trial that merely raises serum magnesium.

Iron trials need clearer definitions of deficiency, consistent retreatment protocols, longer follow-up, and head-to-head comparisons of ferric formulations. Selenium trials need to separate selenium from coenzyme Q10, enroll participants across baseline-status strata, and prespecify safety boundaries. Zinc and copper trials need event-relevant outcomes and systematic monitoring of their reciprocal interaction.

Toxic-metal research should prioritize source-reduction interventions—lead-safe housing, water remediation, occupational controls, smoking cessation, safer food practices—and measure cardiovascular outcomes, not just blood or urine changes. Trials of chelation for cardiovascular disease would need to identify the causal metal, use modern background therapy, include renal and mineral safety outcomes, and demonstrate benefit beyond biomarker depletion.

Monitoring science also requires standardization. Plasma, serum, whole blood, urine, hair, and tissue measures should not be treated as interchangeable. Assays need validated pre-analytic procedures, age- and sex-appropriate reference intervals, and clinically meaningful thresholds. The absence of a validated therapeutic threshold is itself a reason to avoid routine concentration manipulation.

The overall judgment is therefore conditional rather than categorical. Metal modulation is an effective clinical principle when it corrects a defined deficiency, treats a genuine poisoning, or supports a narrowly selected heart-failure or perioperative indication. It is not currently an effective general method for optimizing plasma ions to prevent or treat cardiovascular disease.
